title: IBLA 2019-0110 ) DOI-BLM-ORWA-L040-2017-0015-EA (IBLA 2019-0110)

March 3, 2026
IBLA 2019-0110 ) DOI-BLM-ORWA-L040-2017-0015-EA
)
KLAMATH SISKIYOU WILDLANDS ) Invasive Plant Management
CENTER )
) Affirmed
ORDER∗
Appellant Klamath Siskiyou Wildlands Center (KS Wild) filed this appeal from an
April 5, 2019, Decision issued by the Field Manager of the Bureau of Land Management’s
Lakeview District – Klamath Falls Resource Area (KFRA) in Oregon (BLM). In the
Decision, BLM broadened the scope of the KFRA’s weed management program from
noxious weeds to include all invasive plants, authorized additional non-herbicide direct
control methods, and increased the number of herbicides available for use from 4 to 17.
KS Wild alleges that BLM’s National Environmental Policy Act analysis is deficient
in multiple respects, that the Decision is inconsistent with the governing resource
management plan, and that BLM failed to comply with the Endangered Species Act. For
the reasons explained below, we find that KS Wild has not met its burden to show error
in BLM’s Decision and accordingly affirm.
BACKGROUND
A. BLM’s Decision
BLM’s Decision revises its program for the control of invasive plants using
specified herbicide and non-herbicide methods throughout the KFRA (with the exception
of the Tunnel Creek Area of Critical Environmental Concern, where no treatments are
authorized), which encompasses approximately 225,000 acres in Klamath County,
Oregon.1 Invasive plants are “nonnative aggressive plants with the potential to cause

significant damage to native ecosystems and/or cause significant economic losses.”2 Prior
to the Decision, the KFRA had managed weeds pursuant to a 1993 Integrated Weed
Management Plan and Environmental Assessment and Decision Record (the 1993 Plan).3
The 1993 Plan authorized control of only noxious weeds, a subset of invasive plants that
are county, State, or Federally listed as injurious to public health, agriculture, recreation,
wildlife, or public or private property.4 Under the 1993 Plan, authorized non-herbicide
methods included hand-pulling and competitive seeding and planting, and authorized
herbicides included 2,4-D, glyphosate, dicamba, and picloram.5
BLM decided to update and expand the program to authorize treatment methods
that are “generally more selective, provide better control, and have fewer adverse
environmental effects.”6 It explained that despite efforts under the prior program,
noxious weeds were continuing to spread at an estimated rate of 12 percent per year,
and that more selective herbicides were available to treat invasive plants.7 In its
Decision, BLM expanded the list of permissible non-herbicide treatment methods to
include targeted grazing, biological control agents, competitive seeding and planting,
propane torch spot treatments, broadcast burning, and mechanical methods such as
chainsaws and string trimmers.8 The herbicides authorized under the revised program
include 2,4-D, aminopyralid, chlorsulfuron, clopyralid, dicamba, dicamba +
diflufenzopyr, fluroxypyr, glyphosate, imazapic, imazapyr, metsulfuron methyl, picloram,
rimsulfuron, sulfometuron methyl, triclopyr, and limited and controlled use of fluazifop-
P-butyl and Pseudomonas fluorescens.9 BLM explained that these herbicides are “more
selective in treating invasive plants” and “can be used in lower quantities and pose less
environmental and human health safety risk than the herbicides” previously utilized.10

BLM analyzed the effects of its decision within the KFRA in an Environmental
Assessment (EA), which tiers to three earlier Environmental Impact Statements which
analyzed expanded invasive plant management programs at the State or National level.11
In the EA, BLM analyzed two alternatives in detail: the no action alternative and the
proposed action alternative.12
The no action alternative provided for BLM to continue managing only noxious
weeds with four herbicides as provided in the 1993 Plan.13 The proposed action
alternative provided for BLM to expand the scope of the program to all terrestrial
invasive plants and increase the permissible treatment methods to include the non-
herbicide and herbicide methods described above.14 BLM estimated that the availability
of the additional herbicides would increase the effectiveness of the average treatment
from 60 to 80 percent.15 BLM explained that would it treat approximately 1,200 gross
acres (90 net acres) with herbicide annually, and that the majority of treatments would
continue to be by non-chemical methods, primarily manual.16 It stated that more than a
third of the herbicide treatments would use aminopyralid, which is effective on
starthistles, thistles, and knapweeds, or imazypic, which is effective on annual grasses
and leafy spurge.17
Treatments are limited to the application rates set forth in Table B-6 of the EA,
which specifies the typical and maximum application rates for each herbicide,18 and
constrained by the protection measures set forth in Appendix A.19
BLM’s Decision provides for implementation and effectiveness monitoring to
continue pursuant to U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requirements and BLM
policy, and for data to be recorded in the National Invasive Species Information
Management System (NISIMS) database.20 BLM’s Decision also requires additional
monitoring. For example, the Decision provides for close monitoring of “special status
plant communities,” for the first three to five years of implementation.21 It also provides
for monitoring of targeted grazing to control the timing and intensity of the grazing, and

Following public scoping in May 2017, BLM released the 185-page (including
appendices) EA for a 30-day public comment period in December 2018.23 BLM received a
single comment letter during scoping and a single comment letter during the public
comment period, both from KS Wild.24 BLM determined that the comments did not
provide any substantially new information or new analysis, or identify any significant
new data which would alter the effects described in the EA.25 BLM issued its Decision
approving the program and a Finding of No Significant Impact on April 5, 2019, and
mailed a copy of both to KS Wild along with a summary of KS Wild’s comments and
BLM’s responses.26 In the Decision Record, BLM explained that prior to the beginning of
control treatments each spring, the KFRA will develop an Annual Treatment Plan subject
to an interdisciplinary team review and prepare a Determination of National
Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) Adequacy (DNA) based on the EA, if additional NEPA
analysis is not required.27 BLM further stated that these Annual Treatment Plans will be
posted on BLM’s ePlanning website, beginning with the plan for calendar year 2019.28
B. KS Wild’s Appeal
KS Wild timely appealed and filed its Statements of Reasons.29 After filing the
administrative record and a supplement thereto, BLM filed its Answer in July 2019.30
Given the significant amount of time that had passed since BLM issued the
challenged Decision, we asked the parties to confer and submit a joint status report
addressing the status of the Decision and whether any issues raised in the appeal may
have been resolved or had otherwise become unnecessary to decide, among other
issues.31 In their status report, the parties jointly stated that the Decision “is being

We agree with the parties that the appeal remains ripe for adjudication.34
ANALYSIS
A. Summary Affirmance is Not Warranted
Relying on Klamath-Siskiyou Wildlands Center,35 BLM argues that the Board
should summarily affirm BLM’s decision because KS Wild has merely reiterated the
arguments it raised during the NEPA process, and BLM considered and responded to
these comments in the EA Comment/Response Summary.36 In Klamath-Siskiyou
Wildlands Center, however, the Board had before it a denial of a protest to a forest
management decision.37 The Board found that where the appellant merely repeated
arguments raised in the protest without addressing the protest decision, the appellant
had failed to identify error in the decision on appeal.38 Here, there has been no separate
agency decision specifically responding to KS Wild’s arguments akin to the adjudication
of a protest or other similar process. This Board has previously declined to summarily
affirm similar BLM decisions concerning integrated invasive plant management plans in

treat this appeal differently.39 Relatedly, the Department’s recently revised regulations at
43 C.F.R. part 4 provide for the Board to affirm without opinion in specified
circumstances, including when “the bureau or office has provided a level of
administrative review before the appeal to the Board.”40 Here, BLM provided no such
review. For these reasons, we find that summary affirmance is not warranted.
We now turn to the merits of KS Wild’s arguments on appeal.
B. KS Wild Has Not Met Its Burden to Establish a NEPA Violation
KS Wild’s alleges that BLM’s NEPA analysis is deficient in the following respects:
1) the EA is programmatic in nature and does not adequately support the suite of actions
proposed or the Annual Treatment Plans; 2) BLM erred in using data in the NISIMS and
did not provide sufficient location and scale information to permit meaningful public
involvement; 3) BLM failed to comply with applicable adaptive management regulations;
4) the EA is biased against nonnative species and scientifically inaccurate; 5) BLM failed
to adequately analyze the impacts of aerial spraying and targeted grazing; 6) BLM erred
by authorizing the use of picloram; 7) BLM failed to consider relevant information about
glyphosate; and 8) BLM failed to adequately analyze the cumulative impacts of its action
combined with the Oregon Department of Transportation’s spraying of herbicides on
adjacent State highways.41 Before addressing these arguments, we first set forth the
governing law at the time of BLM’s Decision.
1. Legal Principles Governing National Environmental Policy Act Challenges
Section 102(2)(C) of NEPA requires Federal agencies to prepare an
Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) evaluating the potential environmental impacts
of any major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human
environment.42 As it did here, BLM may prepare an EA to assist its determination of

2025); Order, Blue Mountains Biodiversity Project, IBLA 2016-195, Affirmed at 4-5 (Sept.

whether an EIS is required or to aid the agency’s decision-making when an EIS is
unnecessary.43 As it also did here, BLM issues a FONSI when it concludes that an EIS is
not necessary.44
An EA is “a concise public document” that includes “brief discussions” of the
“environmental impacts of the proposed action and alternatives”45 at a level of depth and
detail normally “limited to the minimum needed to determine whether there would be
significant environmental effects” from the proposed action.46 This Board has
consistently held that an “EA need not discuss the merits and drawbacks of the proposal
in exhaustive detail” as by “its nature, it is intended to be an overview of environmental
concerns, not an exhaustive study of all environmental issues”; accordingly, so long “as
an EA contains a ‘reasonably thorough discussion of . . . significant aspects of the
probable environmental consequences,’ NEPA requirements have been satisfied.”47
In evaluating the adequacy of an EA, the Board is guided by a “rule of reason”48
and will generally find that BLM has taken the requisite “hard look” when its conclusion
that no significant environmental impact exists is founded on a reasoned evaluation of
relevant factors that is documented in the record.49 Our task is not to determine whether
an EA is based upon the best scientific data or methodology available, or to resolve
scientific disagreement over those subjects, but rather to determine whether BLM’s
analysis of the available data was reasonable and provides an adequate basis for its
decision.50 An appellant challenging a BLM decision analyzed in an EA “has the burden
of demonstrating with objective proof that the decision is premised on a clear error of
law or demonstrable error of fact, or that the analysis failed to consider a substantial
environmental question of material significance to the proposed action.”51 This burden is
not satisfied by speculation, conclusory allegations unsupported by evidence, or mere
differences of opinion regarding the likelihood or significance of environmental

impacts.52 Nor are disagreements or presentations of different points of view over the
preferable course of action sufficient absent connection to an affirmative showing that
BLM failed to consider a substantial environmental question of material significance.53
The fact that “an appellant has a different opinion about the likelihood or significance of
environmental impacts or prefers that BLM take another course of action does not
establish that BLM violated the procedural requirements of NEPA.”54
BLM is entitled to rely on the professional opinions of its technical experts
concerning matters within the realm of their expertise and which are reasonable and
supported by record evidence, and an appellant challenging such reliance must
demonstrate, by a preponderance of the evidence, error in the data, methodology,
analysis, or conclusion of the expert.55 Such opinions are entitled to considerable
deference,56 and a “mere difference of opinion, even of expert opinion, will not suffice to
show that BLM failed to fully comprehend the true nature, magnitude, or scope of the
likely impacts.”57 Ultimately, NEPA is a procedural statute that requires only full
consideration of the environmental impacts of a proposed action before undertaking it
and does not direct that BLM take any particular action or prohibit action even where
environmental degradation is inevitable.58
2. KS Wild Has Not Shown that the EA is Insufficiently Detailed as a General
Matter or that BLM’s Approach of Preparing Annual Treatment Plans and
Evaluating Them Against the EA is Inconsistent with NEPA
KS Wild argues that the EA is programmatic in nature and inadequate to support
any of the management actions BLM authorized at the site-specific level. 59 It asserts that

Annual Treatment Plan “would need site specific environmental analysis (detailed maps,
site objectives, reasons for selecting specific herbicides at the site, compliance with
relevant BiO[p]s, site monitoring plan) and opportunity for public review.”61 It also
alleges that the 2019 Annual Treatment Plan fails to identify special status species or
map their locations within treatment areas as contemplated by earlier programmatic
NEPA analyses.62 KS Wild effectively argues that BLM could never lawfully conclude that
the analysis in the EA “adequately assesses the environmental effects of the proposed
action and reasonable alternatives”63 of an Annual Treatment Plan, which a DNA for such
a plan would reflect.
At the outset, we find that KS Wild’s challenge to the 2019 Annual Treatment Plan
is moot because it has expired and there is no effective relief the Board can grant KS
Wild with respect to it.64 We also clarify that no other Annual Treatment Plan is before
us in this appeal. When KS Wild filed its Statement of Reasons, BLM had not approved
any Annual Treatment Plan using a DNA. KS Wild appears to have believed that BLM
planned to issue a DNA for the 2019 Annual Treatment Plan,65 but the Decision itself
authorizes the invasive plant control activities planned for 2019, which are set forth in
Table B-5 of the EA.66 The Decision explains that, going forward, before beginning
treatments each spring, BLM would update the Annual Treatment Plan and subject it to
review by an interdisciplinary team.67 BLM further stated that, as necessary, it would
revise the Annual Treatment Plan to comply with the Decision or complete the
appropriate level of additional NEPA analysis and issue a new decision.68 BLM stated that
it would post the Annual Treatment Plans on its ePlanning website,69 and has since

When BLM’s use of a DNA is properly challenged—which it is not here—the
question is whether the supporting record includes a sufficient “evaluation of whether
new circumstances, new information or changes in the action or its impacts not
previously analyzed may result in significantly different environmental effects.”72 The
supporting record for the Decision under review does not contain any such evaluation for
any Annual Treatment Plan that BLM approved subsequent to the Decision. Accordingly,
the Board does not opine on whether BLM’s issuance of a DNA for any particular Annual
Treatment Plan complied with NEPA.
With respect to KS Wild’s broader argument that BLM’s approach of preparing
Annual Treatment Plans and evaluating them against the EA is fundamentally flawed, we
disagree. We address KS Wild’s allegations that the EA is deficient in particular respects
below, but KS Wild has identified no flaw in the EA that necessarily renders it
inadequate for any authorization that might be contained in an Annual Treatment Plan.
By way of background, BLM analyzed the use of 18 herbicides for a wide range of
vegetation management purposes within the 17 western states in a 2007 programmatic
EIS (2007 PEIS) which is more than 1,600 pages long.73 In the resulting record of
decision (2007 ROD), BLM approved the use of the 18 herbicides in the 17 western
states.74 Due to a history of litigation concerning BLM’s use of herbicides in Oregon, BLM
subsequently prepared an Oregon-wide EIS (2010 FEIS), which tiered to the 2007 PEIS
and examined the effects of the 18 herbicides at the State-wide level.75 The resulting
record of decision (2010 ROD) authorized BLM districts in the State to consider, through

Then, in 2016, BLM prepared another programmatic EIS (2016 PEIS) analyzing the use

The EA tiers to all of these NEPA analyses, and thus does not analyze the effects
of any of the herbicides authorized in BLM’s Decision in the first instance.79 In it, BLM

does not specify “mapped locations of the proposed actions for 2019 and beyond” or

The management actions BLM authorized are narrow and constrained by
numerous protection measures, including project design features, conservation measures
specified in the 2007 and 2016 PEISs, their accompanying Biological Opinions, and the
2010 ROD, standard operating procedures and mitigation measures, and invasive species
prevention measures.88 For each herbicide, for example, BLM identified its target
invasive species, the areas where its registered use is appropriate, whether it could be
aerially sprayed, and its typical and maximum application rates.89 BLM also provided a
guide for herbicide rotation in the event of herbicide resistance.90 And while the 2019
Annual Treatment Plan is not before us, it is instructive in that it further identifies the
specific areas BLM planned to treat, the treatment objective for each area, the treatment
method(s) that would be used, and the number of acres that would be treated.91
While KS Wild complains generally about this District-level approach, it has not
shown that the approach was fundamentally inadequate for BLM to “fully comprehend
the true nature, magnitude, or scope of the likely impacts” of its action.92
3. KS Wild Has Not Shown that BLM Erred in Using NISIMS Data or Provided

9. KS Wild Has Not Shown that BLM’s Cumulative Impacts Analysis is Inadequate
KS Wild references a 2018 incident in which the Oregon Department of
Transportation (ODOT) sprayed aminocyclopyrachlor on ODOT’s rights of way in La
Pine, Oregon, and argues that BLM erred by not analyzing the cumulative impacts of its
action and ODOT’s spraying of herbicides.178 BLM acknowledges the incident, which
occurred outside the KFRA, but represents that Oregon banned the use of the herbicide
on rights of way in September 2018.179 KS Wild has not disputed BLM’s representation.
The regulations in effect at the time of BLM’s Decision required agencies to
consider cumulative impacts, which were defined as “the incremental impact of the
action when added to other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions.”180
The Board has long held that, to demonstrate a deficiency in BLM’s cumulative impacts
analysis, “it is not sufficient merely to note the existence of other . . . projects . . . without
concretely identifying the adverse impacts caused by such other . . . projects to which the
action being scrutinized will add.”181
BLM addressed cumulative effects in the EA but did not include ODOT’s spraying
of aminocyclopyrachlor.182 Given that the incident did not occur within the KFRA and
that Oregon had banned its use on rights of ways when BLM conducted its analysis—
such that its use was neither present nor reasonably foreseeable at the time—we find no
error in BLM’s exclusion of ODOT’s spraying of the herbicide from its analysis. To the
extent KS Wild suggests that BLM was required to consider the spraying of other
herbicides by ODOT, it has not clearly identified such projects, much less concretely
identified their adverse impacts.
We find that KS Wild has not shown error in BLM’s cumulative impacts analysis.

D. KS Wild Has Not Established an Endangered Species Act Violation
KS Wild argues that BLM “failed to consult with [FWS] about targeted grazing”
and states that the “ARBO II does not address targeted grazing.199 Presumably, KS Wild
means to assert a violation of Section 7(a)(2) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA),
which requires agencies to consult with the United States Fish and Wildlife Service
(FWS) or the National Marine Fisheries Service to “insure that any action authorized,
funded, or carried out . . . is not likely to jeopardize the continued existence of any
endangered species or threatened species or result in the destruction or adverse
modification of [critical] habitat of such species.”200
At the time of BLM’s Decision, six Federally listed species and/or critical habitat
units were known to occur within the analysis area.201 Where a listed species may be
present in the area of a proposed action, BLM is generally directed to prepare a
Biological Assessment to evaluate the “potential effects of the action on listed . . . species
and designated . . .critical habitat and determine whether any such species or habitat are
likely to be adversely affected by the action,” and whether formal consultation is
required.202 Informal consultation is required when the proposed action may affect but is
not likely to adversely affect a species, and formal consultation is required when the
proposed action may affect and is likely to adversely affect the species.203 In the former
circumstance, the proposed action may go forward when FWS concurs in BLM’s not
likely to adversely affect determination; in the latter circumstance, the proposed action
may go forward when FWS prepares a Biological Opinion concluding that the action will
not result in jeopardy to the species.204
Prior to its Decision, BLM had consulted with FWS on numerous prior actions
involving invasive plant management, including the 2007 ROD, the 2010 ROD, and the
2016 SWORMP.205 In 2013, another consultation culminated in a Programmatic
Biological Opinion for Aquatic Restoration Activities in the States of Oregon, Washington

a “no effect” determination for the Oregon spotted frog based on the various protective

CONCLUSION
Based on the above, we hold that KS Wild failed to carry its burden to establish
any clear error of law or demonstrable error of fact in BLM’s April 5, 2019, Decision
broadening the scope of the KFRA’s invasive species management program. KS Wild has
not shown that the Decision violates the procedural requirements of NEPA, is
inconsistent with the governing resource management plan, or that BLM violated the
ESA. Accordingly, we affirm BLM’s Decision.
